Lessons.Title: Comparing Data Sets
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: compare numerical distributions using measures of center, standard deviation and IQR, then justify a context-sensitive decision. This is first-party original Edulytiks material aligned with Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 1 Lesson 15, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/1/15/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). Publisher roles: Building On HSS-ID.A.1; Addressing HSS-ID.A.1 and HSS-ID.A.2; Building Towards HSS-ID.A.2.

Original hypothetical scores from five games per person: Player A scores 100,110,120,130,140; Player B scores 118,119,120,121,122. Both means and medians equal 120, but A has greater variability. Using population SD: A σ=sqrt((400+100+0+100+400)/5)=sqrt(200)≈14.14; B σ=sqrt((4+1+0+1+4)/5)=sqrt(2)≈1.41 points.

Using the median-of-halves convention, A quartiles are 105 and 135 (IQR 30); B quartiles are 118.5 and 121.5 (IQR 3). The first player offers higher peaks but greater risk; the second is more consistent. Which player is preferable depends on a decision-maker's stated objective and cannot be reduced to a single universally best score.

Student task: draw both dot plots on one score axis, independently calculate centers and spreads, and recommend a player for each of two differently stated team goals. Compare why a higher maximum versus consistency could matter and critique a peer's numerical support. These datasets are original examples rather than exact publisher bowling diagrams; the source also asks students to interpret marathon-time groups.

Teacher-scored rubric: 0–2 points each for accurate means/medians, accurate IQR/SD, a comparison using common axes and units, and a defensible choice with stated goal and critique (maximum 8). Player-selection reasoning is human reviewed, not automatically graded as one fixed preference.

Source-activity A/B review, IM Algebra 1 First Edition U01:L15: Source asks choose bowlers from 25-game histograms; invented five-game alternatives are examples, not measured source values. Keep original first-party mathematical material and graphics; source artwork identity is NOT claimed. All physical/technology/partner work remains NOT_PERFORMED unless observed.

KeyConcepts.Title: Center versus spread
KeyConcepts.Definition: Mean and median summarize location, while IQR and standard deviation quantify variability.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Equal means do not imply equal ranges or distributions.
KeyConcepts.Example: Both players average 120, but one has population SD about 14.14 and the other 1.41.

KeyConcepts.Title: Decision criterion
KeyConcepts.Definition: A preference must be justified according to a stated outcome or risk objective.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Name consistency versus occasional high score before selecting a player.
KeyConcepts.Example: A reliability-focused team may prioritize Player B's tight distribution.

KeyConcepts.Title: Comparable graphical representation
KeyConcepts.Definition: A fair visual comparison uses equivalent units, sample sizes and horizontal scales.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Place all scores on the same score axis.
KeyConcepts.Example: Five games per player; score range A 100–140, B 118–122.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare centers
WorkedExamples.Question: Find mean and median for both five-score sets.
WorkedExamples.Method: Calculate sums and ordered middle observations.
Steps: Player A total is 600 across five games; mean 600/5=120.
Player B total is also 600; mean 120.
Each ordered set has 120 at the middle third position.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Both players: mean 120 and median 120 points.
WorkedExamples.Check: Each set has five scores totaling 600.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare population standard deviations
WorkedExamples.Question: Which player has lower population standard deviation?
WorkedExamples.Method: Compute mean-centered squared deviations and divide by n=5.
Steps: A deviations about 120 are -20,-10,0,10,20; squared sum 1000.
Player B is much less variable.
WorkedExamples.Answer: B has population SD about 1.41 points versus A about 14.14.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both calculations use n=5, not n−1.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare quartiles and IQR
WorkedExamples.Question: Use median-of-halves to compare the central-half spreads.
WorkedExamples.Method: Exclude median 120, find each pair's midpoint.
Steps: A lower pair 100,110 gives Q1=105; upper pair 130,140 gives Q3=135.
B lower pair 118,119 gives Q1=118.5; upper 121,122 gives Q3=121.5.
The central half of B is much more tightly clustered.
WorkedExamples.Check: The SD and IQR comparisons agree on which group is more variable.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Choosing a player by mean alone
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Equal mean scores can conceal radically different consistency.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Add a variability measure and specify the team's objective.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a high maximum as automatically best
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: High outliers may be rare and accompanied by larger downside variability.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Comparing differently scaled histograms without checking axes
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use the same horizontal score scale.

SummaryPoints: Center and spread are distinct: both players average 120, while A is much more variable.
A population SD≈14.14 and IQR=30; B SD≈1.41 and IQR=3.
Context determines what counts as a preferable performance profile.
Human-reviewed recommendations require explicit criteria rather than fabricated automatic grading.
